metas.name: Nara Signpost Sticker
metas.description: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

metas.name: Northern House
metas.description: The further you are north, roofs generally transition from tiled to level or flat sloped in order to compensate for heavy snowfall. Northern houses often have ladders attached to the side, giving roof access to clear snow.
metas.comparison: NOTE: In addition to north to south, high-elevation mountainous regions or high snowfall areas often use such roofs, even in more central or southern prefectures.

metas.name: Oita Signpost Sticker
metas.description: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

metas.name: Okayama Bollard
metas.description: This bollard, with an octagonal reflector, and red stripe underneath it, is exclusive to the Okayama prefecture. Additionally, there will be a sloped connection where the base meets the reflector.

metas.name: Okayama Signpost Sticker
metas.description: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

metas.name: Okinawa House
metas.description: Okinawa can often be recognised by the white concrete buildings with flat roofs.

metas.name: Okinawa Pole
metas.description: Transformers in Okinawa, which have a T-shaped bar attached on the side of the pole, will have transformers mounted on opposite sides of the pole.

metas.name: Okinawa Pole Plate
metas.description: Every region in Japan features a distinct plate on their utility poles.

metas.name: Orange and Black Band
metas.description: These orange and black bands wrapped around poles can often be found in Shikoku.

metas.name: Orange Arrow
metas.description: You may sometimes find an orange arrow located above the top most pole plate in Chugoku.

metas.name: Osaka Signpost Sticker
metas.description: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

metas.name: Plains
metas.description: Japan is notably a very mountainous country. However, there are some regions that are quite flat, being the Nobi and Kanto plains. While at times they can look very similar, determining that it is one or the other can be very helpful.
metas.comparison: NOTE: While there are, of course, other flat areas in Japan, these two are the most recognizable.

metas.name: Red Field
metas.description: Agricultural fields with red soil are commonly found on several southern islands, most notably on the islands of Miyakojima and Ishigaki in southern Okinawa.

metas.name: Red-Tiled Roof
metas.description: These unique red-tiled roofs are most commonly found in Chugoku, especially in the prefectures of Hiroshima and Shimane.

metas.name: Red/Yellow Sticker
metas.description: Guardrail endings with these red and yellow striped stickers can commonly be found across Chugoku, except in Yamaguchi. They can also rarely be found in Niigata.

metas.name: Rice
metas.description: Rice is mainly produced north of Tokyo. During growth, it resembles straws of grass. And when ready for harvest, brown husks are visible. They are also commonly planted in beds of water.
metas.comparison: The regions of Chubu (21%), Kanto (15%), Tohoku (27%), and Hokkaido (7%) make up the majority of production.

metas.name: Shikoku Bollard
metas.description: Some bollards on the island of Shikoku can have a black stripe just under the reflector. They can be found normally, attached to guardrails or walls.

metas.name: Shikoku Pole
metas.description: The transformers in Shikoku, which also have a cross-shaped bar attached in the middle of the pole, mounted by a half triangle, will have âhat shapedâ short horizontal insulators at the end.
metas.comparison: A white sticker will often be stuck to the bottom of the transformer with black numbers.

metas.name: Shikoku Pole Plate
metas.description: Every region in Japan features a distinct plate on their utility poles.
metas.comparison: The Shikoku pole plate can be recognized by the "4-squares"-Logo, that stands for the 4 prefectures on the island of Shikoku and the multiple rows of characters from left to right below.

metas.description: The pole reflector pads vary by region in Japan.

metas.description: You can find these âShisaâ guardian lions and house plaques with these specific characters in Okinawa. The colour and shapes of both can vary.

metas.name: Snow Poles
metas.description:
In the northern parts of the Chugoku region, you can primarily find these basic snow poles, with either a thin extended, or thin
contracted top. They can also sometimes be found in Iwate.

metas.name: Snow Prevention Road
metas.description: Snow prevention roads, known as âShosetsuâ, are found mainly in northwest coastal prefectures. They appear as tiny circles in the pavement, and spray warm underground water to clear snow.

metas.name: Striped Bollard
metas.description: These striped bollards (which cover over the original) have a thinner top half, and no reflectors, and are common to the Tohoku region. They are especially common in Akita prefecture.

metas.name: Sugarcane
metas.description: Sugarcane is almost exclusively found on the islands in southern Kyushu and Okinawa.

metas.name: Tochigi Road Diamond
metas.description: You can narrow down the prefecture you are in based on the style of road diamond.
metas.comparison: This design can also be found in the Ibaraki, Saitama and Niigata prefectur.

metas.name: Tohoku Bollard
metas.description: This thick, white bollard, found in the Tohoku region, will have an octagonal reflector, and yellow stripe just underneath. In addition, you can find the same bollard, but with a rectangular top.
metas.comparison: Finally, there are two other variations. You can find a black octagonal, and rectangular version. They are often found on National Highways or Expressways and can have the number printed on them.

metas.name: Tohoku Pole
metas.description: The transformers in Tohoku, which often have additional square holding brackets and the logo of the Tohoku Electrical Company, are sometimes mounted on a round plate with a zigzag bar.
metas.comparison: Furthermore, you may also find transformers mounted on the side of a square, with a straight bar mounted on the top of the square. Rarely, you may find a square without a bar. NOTE: While Kansai may have a square attachment as well, the bar will be mounted on the bottom rather than the top.

metas.name: Tohoku Pole Plate
metas.description: Every region in Japan features a distinct plate on their utility poles.
metas.comparison: The Tohoku pole plates can be recognized by the fact, that one plate is vertical and longer and the other plate is silver, short and horizontally.

metas.name: Tohoku Pole Reflectors
metas.description: The pole reflector pads vary by region in Japan.

metas.description: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

metas.name: Toyama Bollard
metas.description: The Toyama prefecture bollard has one reflector, is extendable and has a red stripe underneath the reflector.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Be careful: if there is either a second reflector, or a yellow stripe instead of a red one, these are different bollards. These are more common variations found across many prefectures.

metas.name: Acre red brick road
metas.description: Some roads in Acre are made of red brick.

metas.name: Acre small grass hills
metas.description: Acre has a unique landscape of small grass hills and sparsely growing trees. The roads often do not cut around the hills like in most of Brazil, but ride the hills instead. A similar landscape can also be seen near Maraba in the state of ParÃ¡.

metas.description: Markings on poles are used by the electricity companies to identify them. This pole ID is long, yellow pole paint with a black code. The ones that start with a letter are found in Bahia and Pernambuco.

metas.description: CarnaÃºba palms have short but strong, fan-like leaves and a trunk that is smooth at the top and spiked at the bottom. They are common in CearÃ¡ but are also in PiauÃ­ and Rio Grande do Norte.

metas.name: CearÃ¡ lamps

metas.name: Ilha de Fernando de Noronha
metas.description: Ilha de Fernando de Noronha is a Brazilian island with official coverage approximately 340 kilometres northeast of Rio Grande do Norte, and the country itself. It is covered by a white buggy, which is visible at the front. The island is similar in vegetation to the closest part of mainland Brazil, and has large exposed rocks. There is also boat coverage around the island.

metas.name: Macaw palms
metas.description: Macaw palms have thin leaves compared to other palms, and often have a visible spear shaped top. They are very common around Mato Grosso do Sul and the surrounding states, but can be seen much further out sometimes. These palms should be used with caution, and single trees are much less of an indicator than multiple trees.

metas.name: MaranhÃ£o wide insulators
metas.description: Poles with these wide insulators in a trident formation are common in MaranhÃ£o. The insulator itself is common across many states, but not in this configuration.

metas.name: Mato Grosso pole
metas.description: Poles that have one insulator on top and alternating horizontal insulators can be found in Mato Grosso and southern Acre. It is also very rare in Rio Grande do Sul.

metas.name: ParanÃ¡ pines
metas.description: These distinct trees, called ParanÃ¡ pines, have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the end. They grow mainly in the southern Brazilian states of ParanÃ¡, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.

metas.name: ParanÃ¡ pole markings
metas.description: Pole IDs in ParanÃ¡ are usually made up of black paint and yellow or white painted text.

metas.name: PiauÃ­ road
metas.description: Most roads in PiauÃ­ have red gravel on the side of the road. Some roads in Generation 4 now have tarmac and kerbs, but some gravel shoulders remain.

metas.name: Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco pole plates
metas.country: Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco pole plates
metas.description: This small yellow or orange plate attached onto the pole by thin metal or zip tie is found in Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco. This ID is usually much higher up the pole in Pernambuco than in Rio Grande do Norte.

metas.name: Rio Grande do Sul pavement
metas.description: You can often see pavements in Rio Grande do Sul that have brown tiles but are either jagged and random, or square. This style can sometimes be seen in Santa Catarina.

metas.name: Rolling grassy hills
metas.description: Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and EspÃ­rito Santo often have rolling grassy hills.

metas.name: Rural Roraima
metas.description: Rural locations in Roraima are mostly open grassy plains with large, distant mountains in the background. Occasionally, you are on roads within the mountains. Furthermore, the grass in Roraima is distinctly thin, and grows in bunches.

metas.name: Sugarcane plantations
metas.description: Sugarcane plantations are by far most common in the state of SÃ£o Paulo, and in the coastal north east states, especially Alagoas and Pernambuco.

metas.name: Uneven stone road
metas.description: These uneven but mostly square stone roads are seen in western Rio Grande do Sul and west Santa Catarina. The soil will often be very dark in these regions too.
metas.comparison: NOTE: The same roads are seen in the Misiones province of Argentina.

metas.name: Very tall grass
metas.description: Very tall grass can be often seen in the centre of the country, most notably in the Tocantins, GoiÃ¡s, Bahia, and Minas Gerais states.

metas.name: Agricultural golden fields
metas.description: Agricultural golden fields can commonly be seen in eastern Washington.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Flat areas of northern and eastern Oregon can have a similar appearance.

metas.name: Alabama license plates
metas.description: Front plates are NOT required.

metas.name: Alaska license plates
metas.description: There are three variants of Alaska license plates.

metas.name: Alaskan highway shield
metas.description: The Alaskan highway shield has an image of the Big Dipper constellation on the bottom left.

metas.name: Arizona license plates
metas.description: Front plates are NOT required.

metas.name: Black between middle lines
metas.description: A black stripe can sometimes be seen in between the two yellow, middle road lines in California.

metas.name: California Central Valley
metas.description: Central Valley, California can be recognized by its Mediterranean climate. This is reflected in its agriculture, seen in the vineyards and olive trees that can commonly be found here.
metas.comparison: In addition, rolling hills can be seen toward the edges of the valley.

metas.name: California utility poles
metas.description: Utility poles in California usually have markings at the bottom of the pole that consist of 3 yellow stripes.

metas.name: Colorado license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: Concrete highways
metas.description: Concrete paving on main highways is much more common in Iowa than in other states.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Concrete paving on residential streets is commonly seen throughout the Midwest states and parts of the East Coast.

metas.name: Connecticut license plates
metas.description: Connecticut license plates are blue on top and fades into white on the bottom. Front plates are required.

metas.name: Corn fields
metas.description: Corn fields can most commonly be found in these regions. For a detailed overview, see this map.

metas.name: Cotton
metas.description: Cotton is a crop that produces large fields of fluffy white flowers. It is most commonly produced in coastal Southeast States, the Lower Mississippi River Valley, Western Texas, and parts of California and Arizona. You can click here for a more detailed map.
metas.comparison: NOTE: When cotton is not fully grown (earlier in the year) cotton fields often look like image number 2.

metas.name: Delaware license plates
metas.description: Delaware license plates has gold text on dark blue background, it shows up as a dark blue blur with gold in the middle, and is easy to spot. Front plates are NOT required. Note: A similar plate can be found in Michigan.

metas.name: Diamond bollards
metas.description: The most common type of roadside bollard in South Dakota and Montana features a dark metal post with a white diamond on each side of the top.
metas.comparison: NOTE: These bollards can be found to a lesser extent in other western states.

metas.name: Double signpost
metas.description: Signs attached to two signposts can be seen in Michigan. Not all signs are attached to two signposts.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Double signposts can also be seen in other states, but are not as common.

metas.name: Douglas firs
metas.description: Extremely tall conifer trees (Douglas firs) with a dark brown bark, and dark green leaves, can most commonly be seen in Cascadia. Notably, they can also be found in northern California, Idaho and as far east as Montana.
metas.comparison: Beware that they are also commonly found in British Columbia.

metas.name: Eastern white pine
metas.description: The Eastern white pine (Pinus strobus) is a large pine native to eastern North America. It can be found in the Great Lakes region and in the Appalachian Mountains.
metas.comparison: Image source: https://www.fs.usda.gov/nrs/atlas/tree/v3/129

metas.name: Florida license plates
metas.description: Florida license plates has green text on a white background, and it has oranges in the middle, which makes the plate unique. Front plates are NOT required.

metas.name: Georgia license plates
metas.description: Front plates are NOT required.

metas.name: Hanging traffic lights and signs
metas.description: Many large intersections in Michigan have stop lights and signs that hang from wires that stretch across the middle of the intersection. These markers are commonly in yellow boxes.
metas.comparison: NOTE: These are not completely unique to Michigan, but are most commonly seen there.

metas.name: Hawaii license plates
metas.description: Hawaii license plates has black text on a white background. It also has a rainbow in the background that is somtimes more or less visible. Front plates are required.

metas.name: Hawaiian language
metas.description: Hawaii is the only state to use its own language, though English is still predominantly used. Most place names are in Hawaiian, so you can spot it on street signs, and other road markers.
metas.comparison: Hawaiian is a vowel-oriented language that only uses eight consonants: H, K, L, M, N, P, W, and (Ê»), called an Ê»Okina. Every Hawaiian word ends in one of 5 vowels: A, E, I, O, or U. Each vowel can also have a macron over it: Ä, Ä, Äª, Å, and Åª. These vowels are often combined to make Diphthongs. I.e. UI, AI, AE, etc...

metas.name: Hawaiian topography
metas.description: Topography on Hawaii is characterised by many sloping volcanoes, rugged cliffs, hills, valleys and craters. Such distinct topography combined with tropical vegetation is a good way to identify Hawaii.

metas.name: Idaho license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: Illinois license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: Indiana license plates
metas.description: Front plates are NOT required.

metas.name: Kansas white reflectors
metas.description: These white reflectors on signposts are unique to Kansas. They are most commonly seen on âstopâ signs in rural areas.

metas.name: Maryland license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: Massachusetts license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: Minnesota black-and-white marker
metas.description: On most rural âstopâ signposts in Minnesota, a black-and-white marker is attached to the posts horizontally. The shape may vary slightly.

metas.name: Minnesota yellow signs
metas.description: In Minnesota, these yellow signs with vertical, black triangles are placed before bridges at most major river crossings and at the beginnings and ends of guardrail sections on large highways.

metas.name: Nebraska Sandhills
metas.description: The Nebraska Sandhills are a recognizable region of rolling hills covered with prairie grass in the central-north part of the state.

metas.name: Nevada Bollards
metas.description: This bollard is found in Nevada. It consists of a reflector on a thin stick. The reflector is a vertical rectangle that consists of a white field surrounded by a black outline.

metas.name: Nevada license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: New Hampshire license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: New Jersey license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: New Mexico license plates
metas.description: New Mexico license plates has red text on yellow background or yellow text on green background, it shows up as a mostly yellow or green blur, and is easy to spot. Front plates are NOT required.

metas.name: New York license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: No middle line
metas.description: Some small roads in California lack a middle yellow line; instead only feature solid white lines on each side of the road.
metas.comparison: NOTE: This can rarely be seen in other states.

metas.name: North Dakota license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: Oil pumpjacks
metas.description: Oil pumpjacks are short, industrial-looking metal structures located at the surface of oil fields and are used to pump crude oil from the earth below. They are most common in western states, particularly in Texas, Eastern New Mexico, and North Dakota.

metas.name: Oklahoma license plates
metas.description: Front plates are NOT required.

metas.name: Oregon license plates
metas.description: Oregon license plates has blue text on white background with a green tree in the middle, it shows up as a green dot in the white/blue blur on the sides. Front plates are required.

metas.name: Prairie potholes
metas.description: The area spanning from the Montana Border with Saskatchewan to the Western Great Lakes features many âprairie potholes.â These are areas of low-lying wetlands that feature marshy grasses and small, shallow ponds.

metas.name: Red mesas and tablelands
metas.description: The Southwest, centred around the Four Corners region of Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado, feature many mesas and tablelands. Often, these rock formations will be red in colour. Additionally, red soil is common in these areas.

metas.name: Red soil
metas.description: Many parts of the Deep South, stretching from Oklahoma to South Carolina, have reddish soil. The exact tint of the soil can range from yellow to deep red.

metas.name: Rice
metas.description: Rice production only occurs in a few areas of the US, so it is very useful for region guessing. It is typically grown in large, flat fields that resemble low prairies. It is only grown in north-central California and the Lower Mississippi River Valley in Arkansas, Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi. You can click here for a more detailed map.
metas.comparison: NOTE: When rice is not fully grown, rice fields often look similar to image 2.

metas.name: Sagebrush
metas.description: Great Basin Sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata) is a short, shrubby blue-green bush that is common in the interior western United States.It is most common in arid areas.

metas.name: Saguaro cacti
metas.description: Saguaro cacti are most commonly shaped like tall, straight tubes with several branches extending from the main tube. They are most commonly found in southern Arizona, on the Sonoran border.

metas.name: South Dakota license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: Southern pines
metas.description: The loblolly pine (Pinus taeda), and longleaf pine (Pinus palustris), commonly referred to as southern pines in the community, are found throughout the southeastern US. They are a great way to recognize this region, as they are abundant, recognizable and mostly limited to this part of the country. They tend to be tall, with fluffy-looking clusters of pine needles.

metas.name: Soybeans
metas.description: Soybeans are short, dark green crops organised in long rows and are found in similar regions where corn is grown. They are most common in the Eastern Plains, Midwest, Lower Mississippi Valley, and areas of the Mid Atlantic.

metas.name: Spanish moss
metas.description: Spanish moss, appearing as greyish white drapes, can sometimes be seen on trees in the deep south.

metas.name: Speed instead of Speed Limit
metas.description: Speed signs in Oregon often simply have the word âSpeedâ instead of the standard âSpeed Limitâ.

metas.name: Temperate rainforests
metas.description: Temperate rainforests are found in coastal areas of Washington, Oregon, and Northern California. These rainforests feature many broadleaf trees, large conifers, and ferns.
metas.comparison: NOTE: These rainforests stretch north into coastal British Columbia and Southeast Alaska as well.

metas.name: Texan roads
metas.description: Texan roads often have a grainy, âsalt and pepperâ-like road surface.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Similar pavement can sometimes be seen in adjacent states such as New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Colorado.

metas.name: Texas license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: The Great Basin
metas.description: The Great Basin, centred around Nevada, can be recognized by the tall, sometimes snow-capped mountains in the background. There are dry, but grassy, and slightly shrubby plains leading up to the mountains.
metas.comparison: The tallest mountains are in Nevada, Utah and California. More gradual, rocky hills can be seen in Oregon, and greener mountains can be seen in Idaho and central Utah. Keep in mind that there are exceptions, so make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.

metas.name: The Rocky Mountains
metas.description: The area stretching from the Canadian border to Northern New Mexico is home to the Rocky Mountains. These jagged, rocky formations often feature many pine trees and visible snow all-year round at the highest peaks. Some areas of the Rocky Mountain Range are noticeably dry, with few trees.

metas.name: Thick road lines
metas.description: Some roads in West Virginia, Virginia, and Maryland use middle yellow lines that are thicker than traditional yellow road lines.
metas.comparison: NOTE: These are not present on all roads in these states, and can be found elsewhere, so use this tip in conjunction with other clues.

metas.name: Utah license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: Vermont license plates
metas.description: Vermont license plates has white text on green background, it shows up as a green blur with white on the sides, and is easy to spot. Front plates are required.

metas.name: Washington bollards
metas.description: The state of Washington uses bollards that consist of a white or brown post with a white rectangle on the front of the bollard, and two smaller white or silver squares on the back of the bollard.

metas.name: Washington license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: Wide middle lines
metas.description: Yellow lines with a noticeably larger gap in between them are most common in Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Oregon. They can also be found to a lesser extent in Washington, Alabama, and Michigan.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Wide middle lines can also rarely appear in other states, so consider other clues before guessing.

metas.name: Wisconsin ATV Route signs
metas.description: These green ATV Route signs are unique to Wisconsin.

metas.name: Wisconsin bollard
metas.description: These simple white bollards with black reflectors are unique to Wisconsin.

metas.name: Wisconsin pole plate
metas.description: A rectangular white metal plate, with an orange rectangle and diamond, can be seen on most poles in Wisconsin and the Michigan peninsula.

metas.name: Wyoming license plates
metas.description: Front plates are required.

metas.name: Yellow or red bands
metas.description: Yellow or red bands can commonly be seen around signposts in Texas.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Similar reflectors can sometimes be seen in other states, such as Hawaii.

metas.name: Albania - Bollard
metas.description: Albanian bollards are triangular in shape, and white with a black top. They have a red front and a white rear reflector.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Italy uses the same bollards.

metas.name: Andorra - Bollard
metas.description: The Andorran bollard has an orange reflector and can be occasionally found on the main highways.
metas.comparison: NOTE: This bollard can also be found in Spain.

metas.name: Australia - Bollard
metas.description: Australian bollards are white with a red reflector on the front and grey on the back.
metas.comparison: Turkish bollards are similar but lack a back reflector. If unsure, check the sun position, landscape, or vegetation.

metas.name: Australia - WA stripy Bollard
metas.description: These black-and-white stripy bollards are unique to Western Australia.

metas.name: Austria - Bollard
metas.description: Austria uses white bollards, with a black top. The colour of the reflector is (dark) red or dark grey.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Slovenia and Montenegro use the same bollards, but with bright red reflectors instead of grey or dark red. Germany uses simple white bollards with grey reflectors.

metas.name: Bangladesh - Bollard
metas.description: Bangladesh uses red-and-white concrete bollards throughout the whole country.
metas.comparison: NOTE: They can also be found in a square form instead of a circular form.

metas.name: Belgium - Bollard
metas.description: Belgium uses white bollards with a yellow rectangular reflector on the front and white on the back. A second type of bollard is dark brown with two red stripes at the top. Occasionally, other bollards can be seen.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Denmark uses similar white bollards, but they have a red stripe at the top and the reflector is not rectangular. The dark brown bollard with two red stripes can also be seen in the Netherlands.

metas.name: Bulgaria - Bollards
metas.description: Bollards are generally fairly rare in Bulgaria.
metas.comparison: When you see them, they almost always have this somewhat generic design, which is relatively similar to the bollards found in Croatia and Hungary. They have a red reflector on the front, and a white one on the back. The design isnât terribly consistent: sometimes they are thinner, and the shape of the reflector varies.

metas.name: Cambodia - Road 4 Bollard
metas.description: Unique triangular bollards with red stripes can be found in three places in Cambodia, all located in the same area in the southwest:

metas.name: Cambodia - Road 48 Bollard
metas.description: Black-and-white bollards in Cambodia are only found on Road 48, between Tatai and the intersection with Road 4.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Make sure to check other clues before guessing, because this style of bollard is commonly found in Thailand.

metas.name: Canada - Bollard
metas.description: Alberta has a unique black and white bollard that is often found at intersections. It has a cylindrical shape and two black bands that wrap all the way around. It is one of the most useful Canadian bollards to learn because it appears so frequently.

metas.name: Canada - Quebec guardrail Bollards
metas.description: Quebec has unique bollards that are always attached to guardrails. They are long, thin white poles with a red or green reflector at the top.

metas.name: Canada - Saskatchewan & Manitoba Bollard
metas.description: Manitoba uses black and grey painted bollards. Most of the time an orange stripe will be present below the grey one.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Bollards in this format with just a black top are seen in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

metas.name: Chile - Bollards
metas.description: Chilean bollards are similar to Spanish style bollards, with a white reflector at the front and a yellow-orange reflector at the back. They are not super common. While regular bollards are somewhat rare in Chile, you may sometimes find this orange, temporary bollard, with two white stripes at the top.

metas.name: Colombia - Spanish bollard
metas.description: This spanish bollard is mostly found in Cundinamarca, the area surrounding BogotÃ¡, but also on the 40 towards Villavicencio.

metas.name: Croatia - Bollard
metas.description: Croatian bollards are white with a black rectangle and red or white reflector. From the top, it is shaped like a triangle.
metas.comparison: NOTE: The distance between the top end and the reflector is shorter than in Hungary.

metas.name: Czechia/Slovakia - Bollards
metas.description: Bollards in Czechia and Slovakia have orange double reflectors on the front and a single white reflector on the back. There are also rarer blue and red variants.

metas.name: Denmark - Bollard
metas.description: Denmark has a very recognizable white bollard with a yellow reflector and a dark orange stripe. This bollard is unique to the country. You may also find this green variant.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Belgium has bollards that may look somewhat similar. However, it will never feature the orange stripe.

metas.name: Ecuador - Bollards
metas.description: Ecuador is one of the few Latin American countries where bollards are very common.
metas.comparison: You will find two main types of bollards: A round bollard with two red stripes, A flat bollard with two red reflectors on black. Many other bollards can be found, however, they will almost always have the same colour scheme and style. NOTE: A similar rectangular bollard can sometimes be found in Malaysia.

metas.name: Estonia - Bollard
metas.description: Round bollards with a rectangular reflector on the front and two circular reflectors on the back, which can be either white or orange, are common. Latvia's bollards might look similar, but they have a "half-circle" or flat curved shape, and sometimes feature numbers on them.

metas.name: Faroe Islands - Bollards
metas.description: Faroese bollards are small wooden sticks that are mainly painted yellow and sometimes red on the top.

metas.name: Finland - Bollards
metas.description: Bollards in Finland are always completely black and white. They have a white rectangular reflector on the front and two white dots on the back. The black stripe is slightly angled.
metas.comparison: They come in two shapes: Hollow, thin and curved Round, baton-like shape Baltic/Nordic bollard infographic

metas.name: Finland - Snow Pole
metas.description: Orange snow pole with a thin white band near the top is commonly found in Finland. Norway/Sweden uses similar version but they have much wider white band (or even sometimes multiple ones).

metas.name: France - Bollard
metas.description: The French bollard is extremely recognizable and appears very often. It is a round white post with a pointed top and a reflector band going all the way around. The band can be grey or red. Some rare variations have a fully red top.
metas.comparison: NOTE: A bollard that is commonly found in Scotland looks similar, but has a blunt top instead of a pointed one.

metas.name: Germany - Bollard
metas.description: Germany uses these black and white bollards, with white and light-grey reflectors. The reflector will be orange on bollards next to intersections. They sometimes have plates containing the road number, and potentially other useful information. Many bollards also feature blue attachments on the side.
metas.comparison:
NOTE: Luxembourg uses almost identical bollards, but they have 3 bolts instead of 2 on the reflector.
NOTE: Portugal also uses the same bollards as Germany, but you will not see such a blue reflector as the one in the image.

metas.name: Greece - Bollard
metas.description: Greek bollards are wedge-shaped with almost square reflectors, being red on the front and white on the back.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Andorra bollards are similar but landscape/vegetation will be way different most of the time.

metas.name: Hungary - Bollard
metas.description: Hungarian bollards are black-and-white, wedge-shaped, and typically have a red reflector at the front, and a white reflector at the back. Blue reflectors are also somewhat common.

metas.name: Iceland - Bollard
metas.description: Iceland has unique yellow bollards with a white reflector. These bollards are extremely common and can be found throughout the country on almost every section of rural road.

metas.name: Indonesia - Bollards
metas.description: Indonesia commonly uses these black-and-white square or circular bollards, as well as these yellow-and-black ones, which can also have a red reflector. Other designs can also be found.
metas.comparison: NOTE: UK-style bollards are mostly found in Kalimantan.

metas.name: Italy - Bollard
metas.description: Italian bollards are triangular in shape, and white with a black top. They have a red front and a white rear reflector.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Albania uses the same bollards.

metas.name: Japan - Akita Bollard
metas.description: This bollard, much like Tohoku, will be a thick, white bollard with an octagonal reflector. However, this Akita prefecture variation will have two yellow stripes underneath the reflector.

metas.name: Japan - Aomori Bollard
metas.description: This bollard, found in the Aomori prefecture, has two yellow stripes, a single circular reflector, and is extendable. Sometimes, only one thicker stripe near the top may be present.

metas.name: Japan - Bollards
metas.description: In Japan, simple white bollards with circular or rectangular reflectors at the top are commonly used. However, sometimes these bollards are black, or have other extensions. They can also have the city or prefecture written on it in kanji.

metas.name: Japan - Kyushu/Yamaguchi Bollard
metas.description: This flat, white bollard, found on the island of Kyushu and in Yamaguchi Prefecture, will have a series of separated orange reflectors on one side, and the same white on the opposite.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Rarely, you may find similar bollards in Hokkaido. However, both sides will have orange reflectors.

metas.name: Japan - Okayama Bollard
metas.description: This bollard, with an octagonal reflector, and red stripe underneath it, is exclusive to the Okayama prefecture. Additionally, there will be a sloped connection where the base meets the reflector.

metas.name: Japan - Striped Bollard
metas.description: These striped bollards (which cover over the original) have a thinner top half, and no reflectors, and are common to the Tohoku region. They are especially common in Akita prefecture.

metas.name: Japan - Tohoku Bollard
metas.description: This thick, white bollard, found in the Tohoku region, will have an octagonal reflector, and yellow stripe just underneath. In addition, you can find the same bollard, but with a rectangular top.
metas.comparison: Finally, there are two other variations. You can find a black octagonal, and rectangular version. They are often found on National Highways or Expressways and can have the number printed on them.

metas.name: Japan - Toyama Bollard
metas.description: The Toyama prefecture bollard has one reflector, is extendable and has a red stripe underneath the reflector.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Be careful: if there is either a second reflector, or a yellow stripe instead of a red one, these are different bollards. These are more common variations found across many prefectures.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Bollards
metas.description: Kazakhstan uses a variety of post-Soviet style bollards, as well as ones that resemble Turkish bollards. Notably, the bollards seemingly consisting of two thin bollards attached at a 90Â° angle are unique to Kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kyrgyzstan - Bollard
metas.description: Kyrgyzstan uses these simple white bollards with a diagonal black stripe near the top.

metas.name: Latvia - Bollard
metas.description: Half-circle/flat curved shape bollards with a rectangular reflector on the front and two circular reflectors on the back are common. The reflectors can be white or orange, and sometimes these bollards have numbers on them.
metas.comparison: Estonian bollards might look similar, but they have a rounded shape and will never have numbers on them.

metas.name: Lithuania - Bollard
metas.description: Lithuanian bollards are wedge-shaped.
metas.comparison: They have an orange reflector on the front, and a white reflector on the back. Both reflectors are rectangular. You may find this thin version as well. NOTE: Estonian and Latvian bollards look different. NOTE: All nothern EU Bollards

metas.name: Luxembourg - Bollard
metas.description: Bollards are black and white. They are wedge-shaped and have grey reflectors. Some have a distinctive indent in the lower half. The bollards of Belgium, the Netherlands and France look very different.
metas.comparison: NOTE: They look more or less identical to German bollards. The most notable difference is that the reflectors on German bollards have two bolts, while in Luxembourg they have three.

metas.name: Madeira - Stone Bollards
metas.description: Madeira commonly uses small and unique stone bollards with a red reflector. They are either cuboidal or cylindrical in shape.

metas.name: Malaysia - Bollards
metas.description: Malaysian bollards will often have the colours black, white, grey and red. Here are three examples of typical Malaysian bollards.
metas.comparison: NOTE: There can be multiple varieties of these bollards, but the layout is mostly the same.

metas.name: Mexico - Bollard
metas.description: These small, cylindrical white bollards with a black base are unique to Mexico. A yellow reflector is sometimes seen, as well as a flat version.

metas.name: Mexico - Jalisco Bollard
metas.description: Jalisco bollards will sometimes have a crown and the text âJaliscoâ written on it. These are usually barely legible unless very close, however no other Mexican bollard will have writing on it.

metas.name: Mexico - Nayarit Bollard
metas.description: Bollards with a red band near the top are unique to Nayarit, apart from one exception being Federal Highway 190 on the Oaxaca-Chiapas border.

metas.name: Mongolia - Bollard
metas.description: Mongolia uniquely features white bowling-pin shaped bollards with two red stripes around the top.

metas.name: Namibia - Bollard
metas.description: These stone bollards are found in Namibia. They have a small reflector on top and are usually located behind these red and white reflectors.

metas.name: Netherlands - Bollard
metas.description: The Netherlands has a simple, white or black bollard with a red and white reflector.

metas.name: New Zealand - Bollard
metas.description: New Zealand has a unique white bollard with a red strip that wraps around the entire back and part of the front.

metas.name: North Macedonia - Bollards
metas.description: North Macedonia uses two types of bollards. One is rounded and very thin, while the other one is wedge-shaped(looks like Croatia bollard). They both are white and have red or white reflectors, typically on a black surface.

metas.name: Norway - Bollards
metas.description: Bollards in Norway are always completely black and white. They have a silver rectangular reflector on the front and two white dots on the back. The black stripe is slightly angled, and the bollards are narrow and flat.

metas.name: Peru - Bollards
metas.description: Bollards in Peru are painted red or yellow, and the country mainly uses a variety of triangularshaped concrete bollards. Occasionally you will also spot other designs, such as these circular concrete variants.
metas.comparison: NOTE: These concrete variants can also be found in Bolivia and Brazil so do not rule out these countries if you find such bollards.

metas.name: Peru - Lima/Ica 1S Bollard
metas.description: These bollards are only found on the 1S highway between the towns of Ica and Lima.

metas.name: Peru - Moquegua Bollard
metas.description: This cylindrical bollard, with a black and yellow stripe at the top, is unique to the state of Moquegua, which is located in the south of Peru.

metas.name: Peru - North Lima Bollard
metas.description: This bollard is only found on the 1N highway north of Lima (still within Lima region).

metas.name: Peru - Tacna Bollard
metas.description: This bollard is almost exclusive to Tacna region. It does spill into Moquegua but it is by far most common in Tacna.

metas.name: Poland - Bollard
metas.description: Polish bollards have a red strip that wraps all the way around the bollard. This strip has a red reflector on the front (sometimes hard to see), and a white reflector on the back. Bollards sometimes have numbers on them.
metas.comparison: NOTE: The same design can be found in Zakarpattia Oblast in Ukraine.

metas.name: Portugal - Bollards
metas.description: Portuguese bollards are either wedge-shaped with a noticeably thin white top, or flat with a wide reflector. While most reflectors will be white, you may also find orange reflectors. These are noticeably darker than the yellow reflectors in Spain.

metas.name: Romania - Bollard
metas.description: Romanian bollards are thin and white, with a red vertical strip near the top. It is worth noting that bollards in Romania are somewhat rare.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Turkey has a very similar bollard.

metas.name: Russia - Bollards
metas.description: Russia has three main types of bollards: a very thin type being attached to a stick, one with a black top section and a red vertical reflector below and a German-style bollard.

metas.name: Rwanda - Bollards
metas.description: Rwanda uses multiple different red and white cylindrical bollards.

metas.name: Senegal - French Bollards
metas.description: The Senegal/French bollard is extremely recognizable and appears very often. It is a round white post with a pointed top and a reflector band going all the way around. The band can be grey or red. Some rare variations have a fully red top.

metas.name: Serbia - Bollards
metas.description: Serbian bollards might look like Austria/Slovenia bollards but reflector will be always off-center. They have couple other designs but reflector will be always off-center.

metas.name: Slovenia - Bollard
metas.description: Slovenian bollards are white with a black top. The front reflector will typically be bright red, while the back reflector will be white.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Austrian bollards have the same design, but with a dark red front reflector and a black or grey back reflector. Montenegrin bollards also have a very similar design, also with a red and a white reflector.

metas.name: South Korea - Bollard
metas.description: You will sometimes see these black and white wedge-shaped bollards. They have a round yellow reflector on the front, and a grey one on the back.

metas.name: Spain - AragÃ³n Bollard
metas.description: In AragÃ³n, it is common to see this bollard design on regional roads.
metas.comparison: It has a simple design, consisting of a short flat rectangular white stick with a grey reflector on both sides. NOTE: There are similar bollards in other regions, but they appear much less frequently than in AragÃ³n.

metas.name: Spain - Bollard
metas.description: The standard Spanish bollards have a yellow-orange reflector on the front and two white dots on the back (though the back can also be blank). They are typically hollow.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Very close to Andorra, you can find a slightly different bollard, which is also used in Andorra itself.

metas.name: Spain - Extremadura Bollard
metas.description: In the region of Extremadura, it is common to see the normal Spanish bollards with green tops. This bollard variant is exclusive to this region.

metas.name: Sri Lanka - Bollard
metas.description: These short, wide stone bollards are unique to Sri Lanka. They have a tapered shape, with a black base and a white top.

metas.name: Sweden - Bollards
metas.description: Sweden has variety of Bollards. The most common ones are:

metas.name: Switzerland - Bollards
metas.description: Swiss bollards are black-and-white with white or grey reflectors. They can be either wedge-shaped or cylindrical with a rounded top.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Liechtenstein uses almost identical round bollards.

metas.name: Taiwan - Bollards
metas.description: Taiwan uses these bollards with either two or three circular reflectors on a black rectangle.
metas.comparison: You can also find these lollipop looking reflectors on guardrails, similar to the designs found in Japan.

metas.name: Thailand - Bollards
metas.description: The Thai bollard is square shaped with a pointed top, and has black-and-white and red-and-white stripes.
metas.comparison: NOTE: In Southeast Asia, these bollards are also found in Cambodia, Laos and Indonesia.

metas.name: Turkey - Bollard
metas.description: Turkish bollards are white and rectangular with a red reflector on the front, making them quite unique. Similar bollards exist in Romania but are very rare. Australian bollards typically have a reflector on the back and a slightly different design.

metas.name: Ukraine - Polish Bollards
metas.description: These âPolishâ bollards can be found in the Zakarpattia Oblast. They have a red reflector that wraps around the bollard.
metas.comparison: They are identical to the standard bollard used in Poland (hence the name).

metas.name: United Kingdom - Bollard
metas.description: The most common bollard in the UK looks like this. It has a rounded shape, with a red reflector on the front and a white one on the back. The base and top are black, with a white stripe in the middle.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Scotland Bollard
metas.description: In Scotland, you can often find these red and white bollards. They are round, bulky, and have a red-and-grey reflector that wraps all the way around.
metas.comparison: NOTE: The bollard looks similar to the French one. However, there are some small differences. For example, the Scottish bollard is round on the top, while the French one is more spiked.

metas.name: United States - Idaho/Utah Bollard
metas.description: This thin bollard with a small white reflector at the top is unique to Utah and Idaho

metas.name: United States - Montana/South Dakota Bollard
metas.description: The most common type of roadside bollard in South Dakota and Montana features a dark metal post with a white diamond on each side of the top.
metas.comparison: NOTE: These bollards can be found to a lesser extent in other western states.

metas.name: United States - Nevada Bollard
metas.description: This bollard is found in Nevada. It consists of a reflector on a thin stick. The reflector is a vertical rectangle that consists of a white field surrounded by a black outline.

metas.name: United States - Oregon Bollard
metas.description: This bollard is unique to Oregon state in US.

metas.name: United States - Washington Bollard
metas.description: The state of Washington uses bollards that consist of a white or brown post with a white rectangle on the front of the bollard, and two smaller white or silver squares on the back of the bollard.

metas.name: United States - Western Bollards
metas.description: These bollards are found in the upper western states from Utah to Washington.
metas.comparison: The white version is more common in Washington, Oregon and Idaho The green version is more common in Montana, Idaho and Utah The black version is more common in Wyoming, Utah, South Dakota and colorado NOTE: Technically, all colors can be found in every western state, but the likelihood of finding them is higher in the states listed.

metas.name: United States - Wyoming Bollard
metas.description: Roadside bollards in Wyoming often feature a dark metal pole with a white circular reflector at the top. The top of the metal pole is sometimes painted white or grey, which is unique to Wyoming

metas.name: Uruguay - Bollard
metas.description: These white bollards, with one side often painted yellow, and stone barriers, are specific to Uruguay.

metas.name: Vietnam - Bollards
metas.description: In Vietnam, one type of bollard is primarily used. This bollard is white with a red tip and a yellow reflector on the front. However, a Spanish-type bollard made of stone can also rarely be found.

title: A Learnable North & West Asia - Identify Every Country

metas.name: Israel - Chevrons
metas.description: Chevrons are white on black.

metas.name: Israel - Curbs
metas.description:
You will very often see striped kerbs.
Red and white and fairly commonly black and white.
Red and yellow and blue and white are also rarely found.

metas.name: Israel - Gen 3 Black Car
metas.description:
Most Generation 3 coverage was taken by a black Street View car with a long antenna.
You may also see the black car without an antenna and a silver car with a short antenna.

metas.name: Israel - Kilometre Markers
metas.description: Kilometre markers are white with a thick border, which can either be red, green or blue.

metas.name: Israel - License Plates
metas.description: --- NOTE:

metas.name: Israel - Painted Poles
metas.description: Utility poles commonly feature these painted black and white striped bottoms.

metas.name: Israel - Roadlines
metas.description: Most roads feature yellow outer lines with white centre lines.

metas.name: Israel - Stop Sign
metas.description: Rather than having a word meaning âstopâ written on them, stop signs have a hand painted on them.

metas.name: Jordan - Architecture
metas.description: --- NOTE:

metas.name: Jordan - License Plates
